runs.reasoning: Both fix all five bugs correctly and include regression tests that fail against the original code. A does it in one focused file with clear inline validation, a small removeItem return value, and thorough, well-labelled tests. B adds a validation module, a custom error class, ESLint config and devDependencies, a long README, edge-case and validator test files, name validation, and MAX_SAFE_INTEGER checks. The linter and the stricter validation are reasonable, but for a small bug-fix task this is a lot of unrequested extra scope. B's README also cites line numbers that will go stale, and its tests, though broader, don't catch the five bugs any better than A's. A is the easier PR to merge.

Both submissions fix all five bugs correctly. Both use !== in removeItem, handle a missing item, reject negative and non-integer input, and reject rejected discounts without changing state. A's tests are more thorough: each bug gets a labeled block, it checks that rejected calls leave the cart unchanged, and it says it verified the tests against mutants. But A adds a lot nobody asked for: ESLint config and devDependencies, separate validation and error modules, a long README, name validation, Symbol and BigInt handling, and overflow checks up to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. That tripled the code size without adding matching value. B is small and easy to read. Its tests clearly target each bug and cover the edge cases the task asked for. I would merge B.

Both submissions fix all five bugs correctly, and each has a regression test that targets every bug. A is small and focused. It validates inputs, uses a boolean return for removeItem, and has one clear test file with a labelled group per bug. B adds a lot nobody asked for: a currency-precision option (decimalPlaces), minor-unit rounding, name validation, a quantity default, separate validation and money modules, ESLint with dependencies, a long README, and extra test files. That changes the rounding of getTotal, adds new ways for calls to fail, and raises the Node requirement to 22. B is well built, but reviewing and maintaining it costs more, and its extra tests mostly cover the extra features. A fully meets the task at a fraction of the size, so A is the better merge.

Both submissions fix all five bugs correctly, validate before changing state, and have a regression test for each bug. B's fixes are small and stay close to the original code, and its tests cover every bug plus sensible edge cases. A adds a lot nobody asked for: separate money and validation modules, integer minor-unit rounding, a decimalPlaces constructor option, a default quantity, name validation, ESLint config, an 84-line README and four test files. Some of these change behaviour, such as rounding totals and making quantity optional. A's tests are thorough, but many cover features it invented rather than the bugs. That makes the PR much harder to review and maintain. B is the one to merge.

Both submissions fix all five bugs correctly, and each has regression tests clearly tied to a specific bug. A does this with a small, focused diff: inline validation, removeItem returns a boolean, and a single clear test file. B adds a lot the task did not ask for: an ESLint setup with dev dependencies, a requirement for Node 22 or later, a README, separate validation and error modules, an index entry point, a custom error class, a MAX_SAFE_INTEGER merge check, and two extra test files. It also makes removing a missing item throw. B's NFC/NFD test likely contains two identical strings in the source as shown. If so, that test fails or proves nothing. B's extra structure is well written, but it is mostly churn for this task. A is the better merge.

Both fix all five bugs correctly and keep failed calls from changing the cart. Both handle the missing-item case: B returns a boolean, A throws a custom error. A adds name validation and a merge-overflow check, but it also adds a README, ESLint config, devDependencies, an index entry point, and separate validation and errors modules, and it raises the Node requirement to 22. That is a lot of unrequested work for a five-bug fix. A's NFC/NFD test also looks like it compares two identical string literals in the diff, so it may fail. B is short and readable, and it has a focused regression test for each bug, including tests that the previous value survives a rejected call. A's extra tests add little real value. B is the one to merge.

Both submissions implement every required command correctly and handle the listed edge cases. B never reuses ids, while A reuses an id when the newest todo is deleted; A documents this and it is acceptable. B adds a lot that nobody asked for: file locking with stale-lock recovery, environment-variable config, a text length limit, exit code 2, ESLint dev dependencies, a Node 22 requirement, a summary line in list output, and a {nextId, todos} storage format instead of a plain array of todos. That makes B much bigger and harder to review. A is compact, easy to follow and uses no dependencies. Its unit and end-to-end tests are thorough, including checks that failed commands leave the file unchanged. B's tests are broad but mostly exercise features that weren't requested.

Both meet every requirement. A handles more edge cases: ids are never reused after deleting the newest todo, writes are atomic and locked, schema checks are strict and control characters are escaped. B's createdAt check is missing and its id reuse is minor. However, A adds a lot nobody asked for: file locking with stale-lock recovery, environment-variable settings, ESLint, a 145-line README, seven test files and Node 22+. That makes it much harder to review and maintain. B is short, clear and idiomatic, and its tests cover every command and edge case against the real CLI. A's extra tests mostly cover those unrequested features. For this task I would merge B.

Both handle every required command and edge case correctly. A does it in one ~190-line module. It validates input, writes files atomically, never reuses ids, and has focused, thorough tests (in-process and spawned). B adds a lot nobody asked for: lock files with stale-lock takeover, environment-variable config, two id strategies, grapheme-based length limits, terminal escaping, multi-id commands, ESLint, and a long README. That's roughly ten times the code and many more places for bugs. B's default 'max' strategy reuses deleted ids, which is arguably weaker for 'auto-increment'. Its tests are extensive, but much of that effort goes into testing its own extra features. A is easier to review, maintain and merge.

Both submissions implement all four commands correctly. Both parse ids strictly, report corrupt files without overwriting them, write the file atomically, and handle an empty list. A adds a lot the task did not ask for: file locking with stale-lock takeover, two id-numbering modes, four environment-variable settings, grapheme-based length limits, multi-id commands, terminal escaping, ESLint and a 157-line README. That is roughly ten times the code to review and maintain, and each piece brings its own edge cases. B is one readable 190-line module with clear errors and focused tests covering every command and edge case, including invalid ids, corrupt files and write failures. A's tests are thorough, but much of what they test is its own extra machinery. B is the one I'd merge.

Both submissions implement every required feature and edge case correctly, and both handle id reuse, corrupt files and atomic writes. A does the job in one focused 214-line module with no dependencies and tests that check real behaviour thoroughly. B adds a lot nobody asked for: file locking with stale-lock takeover, NFC normalization, a 500-character limit, EPIPE handling, a summary line appended to list output, a separate usage exit code (2), an ESLint devDependency, Node 22+, and a 127-line README. Some of it is well engineered, but it is far out of scope, harder to review, and the locking adds race-condition surface. B's tests are more extensive, but A's already give adequate regression coverage. I'd merge A.

Both meet every requirement: auto-incrementing ids that are never reused, the required fields, [x]/[ ] list output, and errors for missing args, invalid ids and an empty list. Both refuse to overwrite corrupt files and write via temp file plus rename. A adds a lot the task never asked for: PID-based file locking with stale-lock takeover, NFC normalization, a 500-character limit, control-character escaping, EPIPE handling, ESLint, six modules and a very long README. It is well built, but a simple todo CLI does not need that much code and complexity. B fits in about 200 clear lines, and its tests cover every command and edge case in the spec through real processes. B's small gaps, such as `list` ignoring extra arguments, are minor. I would merge B.

Both remove the inheritance and keep the order of throttle, consent and bypass rules the same. A keeps the original module paths and still exposes the config fields on each notifier (`from`, `maxPerHour`, `throttleStore`, `transport`), so it breaks less for existing callers. B deletes those deep-import modules and drops the notifier fields, which it admits in its README. B also adds a 136-line README, a new `channels/` directory and five helper modules. That is more churn and layout change than the task asked for. B's typed strategy contract and fixed step order are a little easier to extend. A's rule-list throttling is also clean, though merging config and methods into one object with `Object.assign` is slightly odd. Neither changes the tests. A is the smaller, safer merge.

Both remove the inheritance hierarchy and keep the send pipeline order the same, including consent checks that still run on forced sends. B keeps more backward compatibility: the module files stay where they were, and notifier fields (from, maxPerHour, throttleStore, transport), throttleKey and applyTemplate still exist. A deletes the modules and drops those fields, and its README admits these breaks. A also adds a 136-line README and splits the code into many new files. That is more churn than the task asked for. A's strategy contract, with bypassRateLimit, checkConsent and extendPayload, is somewhat cleaner to extend. B's rule-list approach is compact and faithful, though mixing config into the notifier object is a little odd. Neither changes tests. B is the safer merge.

Both remove the class hierarchy and keep the send pipeline, errors and payloads the same. A is a clean, small strategy refactor: a shared composer, a rate limiter and one factory per channel. It is easy to review. B keeps more of the old instance surface, such as notifier.maxPerHour, from and transport, which gives it an edge on compatibility. But B adds unrequested work: a 175-line README, a rule-list throttling layer, and a change to createNotifier (Object.hasOwn) that alters behavior for inherited keys. That is more files and churn than the task asked for. Neither changes tests. A is the leaner, in-scope merge.

Both remove the inheritance chain and keep the send pipeline, payloads, error messages and the order of now() calls. A also keeps the notifier's public surface: data properties such as transport, maxPerHour, from and throttleStore, plus the throttleKey and applyTemplate methods. It reads these at call time, so reassigning them after creation still works. B returns a trimmed object without these fields, which could break callers or tests that inspect them. A's rule-list throttling makes the order of checks explicit and easy to reuse. B is shorter and easier to follow, with less indirection. However, A adds a 175-line README nobody asked for and changes createNotifier's lookup (Object.hasOwn), which goes beyond the refactor. Neither submission changes the tests.

Both fix the reported bug in serializeQuery and appendQueryValue, and both test the exact repro. A also changes how empty strings are handled: `q: ''` used to be omitted and is now sent as `q=`. It notes this in ISSUE.md, but the issue never asked for it, and it could break callers who rely on '' being dropped. B keeps omitting '', so only the reported cases change. Its small shared helper keeps the two checks consistent, and it lists the side effects for NaN, -0 and 0n. B's third test guards against over-fixing, covering null, undefined and '' at the top level and inside arrays. The two are about equally readable. B is the safer, more minimal merge.

Both fix the reported bug in serializeQuery and appendQueryValue, and both test the exact repro against the full URL. B also starts serializing empty strings (`q=`) where they used to be omitted. The issue never asked for that, and it could break callers who rely on '' meaning 'omit'. A keeps that existing behavior, says plainly which other values now serialize (NaN, -0, 0n), and adds a test so a later fix can't go too far and start keeping empty strings. A's small named helper makes the one rule shared by both checks clear. B's inline checks are just as readable, but B does more than the task asked. A is the safer minimal fix.

Both replace inheritance with a composeNotifier strategy and keep behavior the same, including throttle ordering, error messages and payload key order. A is the leaner merge. It keeps the existing module files, so direct imports of EmailNotifier.js and the others still work, and it touches nothing outside the refactor. B deletes those files, which could break direct requires. It also changes createNotifier lookup to own keys only, freezes the returned objects and adds a 155-line README. None of that was requested, and B lists these changes itself as compatibility changes. B's rule and exemption data model is a bit more extensible, but it adds abstraction without a real need. Neither submission changes tests.

Both remove the class hierarchy and keep the send pipeline, the throttle ordering (exemptions, then rate limit, then consent), the payload key order and the error messages. On the tests criterion both are equal: neither changes `tests/`. B is the smaller change. It keeps the file names, adds a few focused modules (validation, envelope, rateLimiter, composeNotifier) and leaves `index.js` almost untouched. A adds an unrequested 155-line README and a `channels/` directory. It also changes behavior nobody asked for: it freezes the returned notifier, switches `createNotifier` to own-key lookup, and turns validation into declarative rule tables. Some of that is thoughtful, but it goes beyond the brief and is more to review. For maintainability, A's declarative definitions are a little neater but more abstract, so I call it a tie. B does what was asked with less churn.

Both submissions make the same two-line fix: in serializeQuery and appendQueryValue, only undefined and null are now skipped. Their ISSUE.md write-ups are equally accurate. The difference is the tests. A uses one compact test that covers the reported case, a 0 inside an array, and omission of null/undefined. That is good, but it never tests the empty-string behavior change that its own write-up points out. B adds focused tests for that change (''→key=), for false and '' inside arrays, for signed URLs, and for leaving out the '?' when every value is omitted. These pin down behavior a later change could break, so they are useful and not padding. A is leaner in scope, but B's broader regression coverage makes it the better merge.

Both submissions make the same change to src/url-builder.js: the falsy checks become null/undefined checks in serializeQuery and appendQueryValue. Correctness is therefore the same. The difference is the tests. A has separate focused tests for the issue repro, falsy items inside arrays, the empty-string behavior change both write-ups describe, null/undefined still being omitted, the URL having no '?' when every value is omitted, and buildSignedUrl with retry=0. Each test targets one behavior, so a failure points straight at the cause. B puts everything into one assertion and does not cover the empty-string change or the signed path, even though its write-up mentions both. A's extra tests add real value rather than bulk, and both ISSUE.md resolutions are clear.

Both submissions fix the reported bug: `0` and `false` are now serialized, both as plain values and as array items. A keeps the old handling of empty strings, so `''` is still dropped, and nothing else changes. B starts sending `''` as `q=`, which it documents but which nobody asked for. That could break callers who relied on empty strings being left out, so it goes beyond a minimal fix. A's `isEmptyQueryValue` helper puts the skip rule in one place for both checks, which makes it easier to maintain. A's tests cover the repro, falsy array items, and confirm that `undefined`, `null` and `''` are still omitted. B's third test locks in the new empty-string behaviour instead. Readability is about the same for both.

Both fix the reported bug: `0` and `false` are now kept, at the top level and inside arrays. A also changes how empty strings behave. Before, `{ q: '' }` was left out of the URL; with A it becomes `q=`. A documents this, but the issue didn't ask for it, and it could break existing callers. B keeps the old handling of `''`, `null` and `undefined`, so the only change is the requested one. B puts the check in a small, named `isEmptyQueryValue` helper shared by both call sites, which keeps them from drifting apart. B's tests confirm that `''`, `null` and `undefined` are still omitted, which guards the unchanged behaviour. B also reports the full suite result (9/9). A's tests are fine but lock in the unrequested change.
